recent_posts.title: Validating agentic behavior when “correct” isn’t deterministic
recent_posts.summary: Validating AI coding agents like GitHub Copilot Agent Mode is fundamentally broken when using traditional testing approaches, because agent behavior is non-deterministic. GitHub researchers propose a 'Trust Layer' framework that models agent executions as graphs (Prefix Tree Acceptors), merges multiple successful traces using visual and LLM-based semantic equivalence, then applies dominator analysis from compiler theory to extract only the 'essential' milestones every successful run must hit. New executions are validated via topological subsequence matching against this dominator tree, tolerating incidental variations (loading screens, alternate UI paths) while catching real failures. In controlled experiments on VS Code agent tasks, this structural approach achieved 100% accuracy vs. 82.2% for agent self-assessment, and dramatically reduced false negatives in CI pipelines. The framework requires only 2–10 successful traces to build a ground truth model, produces explainable failure reasoning, and is designed to integrate into GitHub Actions workflows.

recent_posts.title: Register now for OpenClaw: After Hours @ GitHub
recent_posts.summary: OpenClaw, an open source framework for building agentic systems with over 350,000 GitHub stars, is hosting an in-person community event at GitHub HQ in San Francisco on June 3, 2026, during Microsoft Build. The evening includes a fireside chat with creator Peter Steinberger, a panel with maintainers, lightning talks, and a happy hour. A Twitch livestream will also be available for remote attendees. Registration is required but does not guarantee attendance.

recent_posts.title: GitHub Copilot CLI for Beginners: Interactive v. non-interactive mode
recent_posts.summary: GitHub Copilot CLI has two main modes: interactive and non-interactive. Interactive mode is the default chat-like session where you can ask follow-up questions and work collaboratively with Copilot. Non-interactive mode uses the `copilot -p` flag for quick, one-shot prompts without entering a full session — ideal for automation or fast lookups. You can also resume previous sessions using `/resume` in interactive mode or `copilot --resume` from the command line.

recent_posts.title: GitHub for Beginners: Getting started with Markdown
recent_posts.summary: A beginner-friendly introduction to Markdown on GitHub covering all the essential syntax: headers, bold/italic text, blockquotes, ordered and unordered lists, code blocks, links, and images. Explains where Markdown is used across GitHub (READMEs, issues, pull requests, discussions, wikis) and provides practical tips like drag-and-drop image insertion and using the Preview button to test formatting before committing.

recent_posts.title: Securing the git push pipeline: Responding to a critical remote code execution vulnerability
recent_posts.summary: GitHub's CISO details how the company responded to a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-3854) reported by Wiz researchers on March 4, 2026. The flaw allowed any user with push access to execute arbitrary commands on GitHub servers by injecting unsanitized characters via git push options into internal metadata. GitHub validated, fixed, and deployed a patch to github.com in under two hours, and forensic investigation confirmed no exploitation occurred. GitHub Enterprise Server customers are urged to upgrade to patched releases immediately. The post also covers defense-in-depth improvements, including removing an unnecessary code path from environments where it shouldn't exist.

recent_posts.title: An update on GitHub availability
recent_posts.summary: GitHub's CTO Vlad Fedorov addresses two recent incidents — a merge queue regression on April 23 that corrupted squash merges in 230 repositories, and an Elasticsearch overload on April 27 that disrupted search-backed UI features. He explains that GitHub is scaling from a 10X to 30X capacity target, driven by explosive growth in agentic development workflows since late 2025. Reliability improvements include isolating critical services, reducing single points of failure, migrating performance-sensitive code from Ruby to Go, moving to public cloud and pursuing multi-cloud, and optimizing merge queue and large monorepo handling. GitHub also committed to greater transparency via updated status pages and proactive incident communication.

recent_posts.title: GitHub Copilot is moving to usage-based billing
recent_posts.summary: GitHub Copilot is transitioning all plans to usage-based billing starting June 1, 2026. Premium request units (PRUs) will be replaced by GitHub AI Credits, calculated based on token consumption. Base plan prices remain unchanged — Pro at $10/month, Pro+ at $39/month, Business at $19/user/month, and Enterprise at $39/user/month — with each plan including an equivalent monthly AI Credits allotment. Code completions and Next Edit suggestions remain free and won't consume credits. Business and Enterprise customers get promotional increased credits for June–August to ease the transition. Admins gain new budget controls at enterprise, cost center, and user levels, plus pooled usage across organizations. A preview billing experience launches in early May so users can see projected costs before the switch.

recent_posts.title: Changes to GitHub Copilot Individual plans
recent_posts.summary: GitHub is pausing new sign-ups for Copilot Pro, Pro+, and Student plans, tightening usage limits, and removing Opus models from Pro plans. The changes are driven by agentic workflows consuming far more compute than the original plan structure anticipated — parallelized, long-running sessions now regularly exceed plan costs. Two types of limits exist: session limits (peak load protection) and weekly token-based limits (cost control). Usage visibility is being added to VS Code and Copilot CLI. Existing subscribers who are unhappy can cancel and receive a refund for April usage by contacting support before May 20.

recent_posts.title: Highlights from Git 2.54
recent_posts.summary: Git 2.54 (covering 2.53 and 2.54) introduces several notable features. A new experimental `git history` command simplifies targeted history rewrites with `reword` and `split` subcommands, without touching the working tree. Config-based hooks allow defining and sharing hooks across repositories via gitconfig files, supporting multiple hooks per event. Geometric repacking is now the default strategy for `git maintenance run`. Other improvements include `git add -p` usability enhancements, HTTP 429 retry support, `git log -L` compatibility with pickaxe options, incremental MIDX compaction, `git rebase --trailer`, Unicode alias names, and `git blame --diff-algorithm`.

recent_posts.title: Building an emoji list generator with the GitHub Copilot CLI
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough of building a terminal-based emoji list generator using the GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot SDK, OpenTUI for the terminal interface, and clipboardy for clipboard access. The project was planned using Claude Sonnet in Copilot's plan mode, then implemented with Claude Opus, resulting in a small CLI app that converts bullet points into emoji-prefixed lists and copies the result to the clipboard.
